content:
A recurring argument against the Quran holds that it contains grammatical mistakes, and that a book with mistakes cannot meet its own challenge to produce anything like it. The argument rests on a handful of verses and on one report attributed to A'isha.

The verses usually named are 4:162, where one phrase in a list of believers takes an unexpected case ending; 5:69, where the Sabians stand in the nominative after a particle that normally takes the accusative; and 20:63, where a dual form seems to ignore the same particle. Behind them stands a larger claim. If the Arabic of the Quran can be faulted, its challenge to produce a sura like it loses its force, and with it one of the oldest arguments Muslims give for its origin.

The four points below take the challenge first and then the verses the critics cite, with what the classical commentators said about each.

The Quran tells those in doubt about it to bring a single chapter (sura) like it, and to call on their helpers other than God, if they are truthful.[1] Another verse states that if humans and jinn joined forces to produce something like the Quran, they would fail, even if they backed one another.[2]

Critics answer that a text full of grammatical faults cannot be a model of eloquence, and they name three verses. The challenge stands or falls on those examples, so each is taken below as the critics present it.

The first audience is the obvious test. The opponents of the Prophet in Mecca spoke the language as natives and prized poetry above every other art, and the Quran records what they said against it: that its reciter was a soothsayer, a madman or a poet, that it was magic handed down from others, or that it was muddled dreams he had made up.[3] Each of those charges concedes the force of the language. Men who wanted the message discredited, and who would have heard a faulty case ending at once, called it magic and poetry. A complaint about its grammar would have been the easiest charge of all to make and to prove, and the sources record nobody making it.

The strongest reply is that listeners in the seventh century did not measure speech against written rules, because the rules had not yet been written, so their silence proves nothing about grammar. That reply concedes the point the last entry makes. The standard was the living usage of the Arabs, and by that standard the first hearers of the Quran found its language so far above the ordinary that they reached for the word magic.

In 4:162 a list of believers runs in the nominative case, then one phrase, wa al-muqimina al-salat (and those who establish prayer), appears in the accusative, before the list returns to the nominative. Al-Tabari recorded the report that A'isha, asked about this verse, about 5:69 and about 20:63, said that it was the work of the scribes, who made errors in writing.[4]

Al-Tabari rejected the scribal-error explanation. He noted that the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b read the same way, and argued that if a scribe had erred, the other codices would differ from ours. He added that the Companions who taught the Quran would have corrected any fault in recitation, and that the whole community transmitted the reading as written.[5]

He also recorded the explanation of grammarians of Kufa and Basra: Arabs shift the case of a descriptive phrase to single it out for praise (nasb ala al-madh, the accusative of praise) when a description grows long, citing 2:177, where al-sabirina (the patient) stands in the accusative within a nominative list.[4] Al-Tabari preferred a third reading, in which the phrase is genitive and refers to the angels, but none of the options he weighed requires an error.[5]

Al-Qurtubi gathered the same discussion two centuries later and judged the view of Sibawayh the soundest: al-muqimina is an accusative of praise, a construction Sibawayh treated in its own chapter of his grammar.[6] Al-Qurtubi also recorded a second report, attributed to Aban, a son of the caliph Uthman, which says that a scribe took down the verse up to "and the believers", asked what to write next, and was told "and those who establish prayer", which he wrote as he heard it. He then quoted the verdict of al-Qushayri on every explanation of this kind: the approach is false, because the men who gathered the Quran were masters of the language, and they would not have set down in it anything that had not been revealed.[6]

The A'isha report has a further limit. On its own terms it blames the scribes for how the words were written. The Quran was taught by recitation, and al-Tabari's answer rests on that fact: the verse was recited in the accusative by those who had learned it from the Prophet, and the community carried that recitation independently of any copyist.[5] A scribe can misspell a word. A community reciting from memory does not take its pronunciation from his pen.

Critics hold that after inna the demonstrative should be hadhayni, in the accusative, and that hadhani is wrong. The Hafs reading, printed in the standard Medina text, reads in hadhani la-sahirani (these two are surely sorcerers), with the lightened particle in, after which the nominative is regular.[7]

The variant readings show the verse travelling through the generations by mouth. Of the seven readers whose readings became canonical, most recited inna hadhani with the stressed particle; Hafs from Asim and Ibn Kathir of Mecca recited the lightened in; and Abu Amr of Basra recited inna hadhayni, with the accusative the critics ask for.[8] The Uthmanic copies carried no vowel signs, and all three readings fit the same letters on the page.

That has a consequence for the objection. The regular form was known and recited in Basra in the second century of Islam by one of the most respected teachers of the Quran. The other teachers kept hadhani beside it because that was how each had received the verse, and because the speech of the Arabs supplied a dialect in which it is regular. A reading kept against the easier alternative, by teachers who knew the alternative, is evidence that they regarded it as sound Arabic.

For the readers who pronounced inna, al-Tabari explained the form as the usage of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am, Zubayd and neighbouring Yemeni tribes, who keep the dual in -ani in every case. He cited verse in that dialect and quoted Abu Ubayda's report that he had heard tribes of Kinana do the same.[9]

The deeper problem with the objection is one of sequence. The rules against which critics measure these verses were compiled by grammarians who took the Quran and pre-Islamic poetry as their evidence. Al-Tabari's discussion of 4:162 and 20:63 shows the method: when a construction seemed irregular, scholars looked for the same usage in the speech of the Arabs, and found it.[5][9]

The treatment of 5:69 shows the method at work. There al-sabi'una stands in the nominative after inna, where 2:62 and 22:17 have the accusative al-sabi'ina in the same list. Al-Qurtubi reports the explanation of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, the founders of Arabic grammar: the nominative is carried by a change of order, so that the Sabians and the Christians are placed under the same promise as the believers and the Jews, with the predicate understood for them.[10] He gives the line of poetry Sibawayh cited for the pattern, "otherwise know that we, and you, are wrongdoers as long as we remain in discord", and a second from the poet Dabi' al-Burjumi, "whoever spends the evening with his saddle in Medina, I and Qayyar are strangers there", in which Qayyar, the poet's camel, stands in the nominative after inna exactly as the Sabians do. Al-Farra, al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash offered other analyses, and al-Qurtubi sets them out. None of them treats the verse as a mistake.[10]

The strongest form of the objection says that this is circular: the grammarians built their rules from the Quran, so the Quran will always pass them. The poetry answers it. The poems the grammarians quoted were composed by people who had never heard the Quran, and they were collected as an independent witness to the language. When a Quranic construction looks irregular and the same construction appears in a poem of the Jahiliyya, the evidence for its correctness comes from outside the Quran.

A further point follows. The rules a modern learner meets in a textbook are the common patterns, distilled for teaching. The grammarians who wrote the first books knew that the speech of the Arabs was wider than the patterns, and they recorded the rarer usages with their witnesses. Measuring the Quran against the textbook, and calling everything outside it an error, reverses the order in which the evidence was gathered.

The bottom line

The grammatical-error argument rests on a handful of verses and two early reports. The classical scholars examined every one of them, and they did so from the same sources the critics now cite. The constructions in 4:162, 5:69 and 20:63 are attested in the speech and poetry of the Arabs. The variant readings show that the teachers of the Quran knew the regular forms and kept the forms they had received. The reports about scribes concern writing, and the leading commentators rejected them as an account of the text.

The first hearers of the Quran had every reason to fault its language and every ability to do so, and they called it magic instead. That proves nothing about the source of the Quran on its own. It does mean that the challenge in 2:23 cannot be set aside by pointing to these verses. A reader who wants to answer it still has to do what the challenge asks.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:23.
  2. Quran 17:88.
  3. Quran 52:29–30; 74:24; 21:5.
  4. Al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, commentary on Quran 4:162, report no. 10838 (Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath edition, Shamela text, vol. 9, p. 395; Hisham ibn Urwa from his father, from A'isha).
  5. Ibid., commentary on Quran 4:162, al-Tabari's own assessment following report no. 10838.
  6. Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, commentary on Quran 4:162, including the report attributed to Aban ibn Uthman and the judgement of al-Qushayri.
  7. Quran 20:63, Hafs an Asim reading as printed in the standard Medina text.
  8. Ibn Mujahid, Kitab al-Sab'a fi al-Qira'at, on Quran 20:63; compare al-Tabari, commentary on Quran 20:63.
  9. Al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, commentary on Quran 20:63, section on the variant readings. Tabari (Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath edition, Shamela text): vol. 18, pp. 326–328.
  10. Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, commentary on Quran 5:69, giving the views of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, al-Farra, al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash, with the verses of poetry cited for each.
